speaker: Jim Keller
title: Jim Keller: Moore's Law, Microprocessors, and First Principles (#70)
question: In processor and complex hardware engineering, why do established companies so strongly resist rewriting an aging architecture from scratch?
guest: To get to the next level, you have to do a new project, and the initial starting point will be lower than the old optimization point, even though it'll eventually get higher. So now you have two kinds of fear: short-term disaster and long-term disaster. People with a quarter-to-quarter business objective are terrified about changing everything. People who are trying to run a business or build a computer for a long-term objective know that the short-term limitations block them from long-term success. If you look at leaders of companies that had really good long-term success, every time they saw that they had to redo something, they did. Or you do multiple projects in parallel, where you optimize the old one while you build a new one. But the marketing guys are always like, "Promise me that the new computer is faster on every single thing." And the computer architect says, "Well, the new computer will be faster on average, but there's a distribution of results in performance, and you'll have some outliers that are slower." That's very hard because they have one customer who cares about that one.

points.core: A clean-slate architecture initially performs worse than a mature optimized design.
points.note: Accept: S-curve transition mechanics where a brand-new architecture starts below the mature legacy design before surpassing it. Do not credit: generic statements that rewrites are expensive or risky.

points.core: Quarterly business incentives make leaders fear short-term disruption over long-term stagnation.
points.note: Accept: short-term/quarterly revenue or schedule pressure causing executives to avoid near-term regressions even at the cost of long-term competitiveness. Do not credit: vague complaints about corporate bureaucracy.

points.core: New architectures raise average speed across a performance distribution with slower outliers.
points.note: Accept: explaining that architectural changes shift a workload performance distribution—improving average/geomean speed while regressing on specific edge-case workloads. Do not credit: claiming rewrites are simply buggy or unfinished.

points.core: Commercial teams demand universal speedups because key customers care about specific workloads.
points.note: Accept: sales/marketing pressure requiring zero regressions across all benchmarks because individual major customers depend on specific outlier workloads. Do not credit: generic claims that customers resist change.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Mostly because the old design's real value is not its elegance but the enormous body of accumulated, hard-won correctness and compatibility wrapped around it.

A mature architecture embodies decades of bug fixes, corner-case handling, and undocumented behaviors that software has quietly come to depend on. A clean-sheet design throws that away and reintroduces risk everywhere. Verification, not design, dominates the cost of modern chips, and existing test suites, validation infrastructure, and formal proofs are tied to the current design; a rewrite means re-verifying everything, and a single escaped bug in silicon can cost hundreds of millions (Intel's Pentium FDIV bug being the classic example).

Then there is the ecosystem: operating systems, compilers, drivers, toolchains, and customer binaries all assume the existing behavior. Breaking compatibility strands customers and gives them a reason to evaluate competitors, as Intel's Itanium showed against the backward-compatible x86-64.

Finally, rewrites take years, during which the old product must still be maintained and competitors keep shipping. Incremental evolution delivers predictable gains on schedule, so companies prefer to extend, layer, and translate (for example, decoding legacy instructions into internal micro-ops) rather than start over.

points.why: The response describes lost correctness and verification work but never says a clean-slate design initially performs worse than the optimized legacy design.
The response cites lengthy rewrites and predictable release schedules but does not connect short-term business incentives to accepting long-term stagnation.
The response never explains that a new architecture can improve average performance while slowing specific workloads.
The response discusses customers' dependence on compatibility but does not explain why commercial teams demand speedups on every workload.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Established hardware companies resist clean-sheet redesigns primarily because an architecture’s greatest value lies in its software ecosystem, accumulated verification, and physical maturity rather than design elegance. Replacing an instruction set threatens decades of backward compatibility across operating systems, compilers, drivers, and customer binaries—a barrier famously illustrated when evolutionary x86-64 defeated Intel’s clean-slate Itanium.

Even when external compatibility is preserved, rewriting hardware blocks and microarchitecture from scratch discards years of silicon-proven fixes for subtle corner cases in cache coherency, speculative execution, and electrical timing. Unlike software, silicon cannot be cheaply patched after fabrication; escaped bugs trigger multi-million-dollar mask respins, months of lost market window, or crippling recalls. Mature designs also carry hard-won physical layouts, power-thermal models, and foundry tuning that a new implementation must painfully rediscover. Finally, ground-up hardware projects demand half a decade or more of massive parallel investment before generating revenue, inviting scope creep while competitors compound steady gains on proven foundations. In silicon engineering, evolutionary refinement almost always beats the existential risk of starting over.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Established companies resist from-scratch rewrites mainly because the old design holds a huge amount of proven knowledge that is hard to see. A mature architecture embodies years of bug fixes, errata workarounds, timing closures, and corner-case behavior that software and customers silently depend on. A new design throws all of that away and has to rediscover it the hard way.

Verification is the biggest obstacle. It typically takes well over half of a chip project's effort, and a clean-sheet core needs new testbenches, validation suites and silicon debug, with each respin costing millions and months. Compatibility matters too: decades of binaries, operating systems, compilers and firmware expect exact behavior, as Intel found with Itanium.

Schedule risk is the next problem. A new microarchitecture takes four to six years, and in that time competitors keep improving their existing designs. Bulldozer and NetBurst showed that ambitious redesigns can launch behind the products they were meant to replace. Teams also tend to overreach on a second system.

So firms usually evolve their designs step by step, refactoring subsystems one at a time and keeping something shippable throughout. They save true rewrites for cases where the old foundation clearly can't scale any further.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Established hardware companies resist clean-slate architectural rewrites because the financial, technical, and commercial risks are extraordinarily high. Modern processors sit beneath decades of software, compilers, firmware, and enterprise workloads that rely not only on documented instruction sets, but also on subtle memory-ordering behaviors and legacy quirks. Breaking backward compatibility threatens the software ecosystem that locks customers in, often making migration a non-starter regardless of hardware elegance.

Equally daunting is the engineering and verification burden. Developing a flagship chip from scratch can cost billions of dollars and take five or more years, with validation consuming a massive share of that effort. Evolving an existing architecture lets teams reuse silicon-proven blocks, mature physical design flows, and hard-won fixes for obscure corner-case bugs. A rewrite forfeits that institutional hardening and invites unpredictable delays.

Finally, there is severe competitive risk. While a company pours its best engineers into an unproven replacement, competitors—and even its own legacy line—keep shipping incremental gains, often leaving the clean-slate design too late to justify its cost.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
An aging processor architecture embodies years of debugging, validation, and compatibility work. A clean-sheet replacement has to earn that maturity again. If it preserves the instruction set, it still has to reproduce subtle behavior that operating systems, firmware, and applications depend on. If it changes the instruction set, customers also need a credible path to move their software.

The cost extends well beyond designing the core. Teams must verify interactions among caches, memory, interrupts, and power states, then prove the chip meets timing, power, and manufacturing targets. A bug found after fabrication can require a costly new silicon revision and delay the product. Meanwhile, the company still has to support existing chips and ship new ones on schedule.

That’s why companies often replace major subsystems over several generations. They can capture much of the performance or efficiency gain while preserving compatibility and limiting how much new hardware they have to validate at once.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
An established chip design embodies years of work proving that it behaves correctly, meets timing and power targets, and can be manufactured economically. Some of that knowledge lives in workarounds for rare failures. A rewrite can discard those fixes while introducing bugs that only show up in silicon, where a mistake can mean another fabrication run and months of delay.

A new internal design can preserve the instruction set and run existing software, but the team still has to verify that compatibility. Changing the instruction set as well raises the cost further because customers may need to migrate operating systems, tools, and applications.

Incremental redesign lets a company replace the parts that limit performance or efficiency, reuse proven components, and keep shipping products while it validates each change. The economic question is whether starting over offers enough advantage over that path to justify the engineering effort, schedule risk, and potential disruption to customers.

The response never explains that average performance can improve while specific workloads run slower.
